title: Make It Longer
theme: Expanding the child's own short message into a longer sentence
materials: No materials needed — use whatever your child is already doing, looking at, or talking about.
instructions: Listen for a moment when your child says something short, such as "dog sleeping" or "want blue car." Answer the meaning first so the conversation stays real — "He is sleeping, isn't he?" Then say the same idea back as a longer sentence with one thing added: "The dog is sleeping." Pause and leave space. If your child says a longer version, warmly repeat it and carry on with whatever you were both doing. Look for three or four of these moments across a day rather than setting aside a practice session.
success_criteria: The child says a sentence of at least four words at least once. The grammar and the articulation do not need to be correct — "the dog is sleep" counts — but the sentence does need to be four or more words.
make_easier: Say the whole longer sentence yourself and leave a pause, or give the first words as a starter — "The dog is..." Add only ONE element to what your child said. A two- or three-word reply is a good attempt and should be warmly expanded, but it is scaffolding and is not yet the four-word target.
make_harder: Wait and let your child lengthen the sentence without a model. Add a second element — a place, an object, a describing word, or another person: "The big dog is sleeping on the floor."
group_play_line: A sibling can say the longer version of what your child said, so your child hears the expansion from someone other than you.
what_to_avoid: Do not ask your child to repeat the model, and never ask twice. Expansion is something you do for your child, not a drill. If nothing longer comes, say the longer sentence yourself and move on.

title: Who Is Doing What?
theme: Describing who is doing what, in a whole sentence
materials: Toy animals or figures, family photos, or a picture of a simple scene.
instructions: Find or arrange one simple scene where somebody is doing something to something — a dog eating food, a girl reading a book, someone washing the dishes. Ask what is happening, or simply look at it together and wait. Give your child time to describe it. Accept a sentence that names who, the action and what — "The dog is eating food" — and warmly say it back once. If only the action word comes, say the whole sentence yourself and find another scene.
success_criteria: The child says a sentence of at least four words describing who is doing what. A single action word such as "eating" is NOT success here — that is action labelling, and this card is about the sentence.
make_easier: Give your child the start and let them finish — "The dog is..." You can also supply the subject and ask for the rest. A two- or three-word version is a real attempt: say the full sentence back, and count the four-word target only when your child produces it.
make_harder: Ask for more inside the same sentence — what kind, or where. "The girl is reading a funny book." "The dog is eating food outside."
group_play_line: Let a sibling arrange a scene for your child to describe, then swap over.
what_to_avoid: Do not interrupt the interaction to correct grammar, word order, or pronunciation. If the sentence needs support, model the natural version back once and continue. Do not keep asking about the same scene; use a new one instead.

title: Add Where
theme: Adding a place to a simple sentence
materials: Whatever is happening in the room, or a picture with a clear setting.
instructions: Notice something happening and say a short sentence about it, then say it again with the place added: "The baby is sleeping. The baby is sleeping in bed." Now look at something else happening and ask your child to tell you about that. Give them time. Accept a sentence that says who, the action and where — "Maya is playing on the floor." Say it back warmly once and carry on with what you were doing.
success_criteria: The child says a sentence of at least four words that includes who or what, the action, and where it is happening. Pointing at the place does not count — the place has to be spoken.
make_easier: Offer two places out loud to choose between — "Is she sleeping in bed or in the bath?" — and let your child answer in a sentence. You can also model the pattern "in the ..." and give the starter. A sentence without the place yet is a good attempt to expand, not the target.
make_harder: Let your child supply the place with no choices and no model. Add one describing word on top: "The little dog is eating in the kitchen."
group_play_line: A sibling can say where something is happening, then ask your child about something else in the room.
what_to_avoid: This card is about making the sentence longer, not about testing whether your child knows place words. If the place word is wrong but the sentence is long, that is still success — say the right word back warmly and carry on.

title: Tell Me What Happened
theme: One sentence about one thing that happened
materials: No materials needed, though a photo or an object from the event can help.
instructions: Ask about ONE thing that happened recently — "What did you eat?", "What did you play?", "What happened at the park?" Give your child time to answer. Accept a sentence about that one event, such as "I played with the blocks" or "We ate pizza for lunch." Say it back warmly once and show you are interested in it. Ask about one event, not about the whole day.
success_criteria: The child says a sentence of at least four words about ONE thing that happened. One event is the whole target — two events, an order of events, or a beginning and an end are NOT required and are not what this card practises.
make_easier: Ask about something that happened minutes ago rather than yesterday. Show a photo, or hold the object from the event. Give a starter — "I played..." A short answer such as "blocks" is a good start: say the full sentence back and look for the longer one another time.
make_harder: Ask with no photo and no object, about something earlier in the day. You can invite one extra detail — "Who was there?" — while keeping it to the same single event.
group_play_line: A sibling can answer about the same event first, so your child hears a whole sentence before taking a turn.
what_to_avoid: Do not ask your child to tell the whole story or to put events in order — that is a different and much later skill. Do not keep asking if your child does not remember; say what you remember and move on.

title: Tell Me Something
theme: Commenting on something interesting, without being asked
materials: Whatever is to hand — a toy, a book, a window, something that has just happened.
instructions: Make something worth remarking on: push a car fast across the floor, build a tower that wobbles, put a hat on a teddy, or notice something out of the window. Say your own comment out loud — "That car is really fast" — then stop talking and look interested. Leave a long pause. Comments come when there is something to comment on and room to say it. If your child comments, answer what they said rather than how they said it.
success_criteria: The child says a comment of at least four words during the interaction, without being asked a question. A comment is a telling rather than an answer.
make_easier: Make the interesting thing bigger and more obvious, and comment twice yourself before pausing. A two- or three-word comment is exactly the right thing happening and should be warmly expanded — count the four-word target when it arrives, and keep playing either way.
make_harder: Say less yourself and wait longer. Make something quietly surprising rather than dramatic, so noticing it is part of the fun.
group_play_line: Two children remarking on the same silly thing will often spark more comments than an adult asking questions does.
what_to_avoid: Do not turn this into questions — no "What do you see?", no "What is that?" A question turns a comment into an answer, which is the opposite of what this card is for. Naming the object is not the point either.

title: Not That One
theme: Saying no inside a whole sentence
materials: Two of something your child has an opinion about — crayons, toy cars, two cups — or pictures, or pretend play.
instructions: Offer two things and let your child pick one. Then play gently at being wrong: hold up the one they did not choose and say "This is the one you wanted." Give them time to put you right. Accept a sentence that says no and says what — "I don't want that one", "That is not my cup." Say it back warmly once and hand over the right one straight away. Pretend play works too: give the teddy the wrong hat and let your child tell you about it.
success_criteria: The child says a sentence of at least four words containing a real negation such as "not", "don't" or "no". The negation has to sit inside a sentence; a single "no" is clear communication but is not this card's target.
make_easier: Model the sentence with the negative word in it — "That is not your cup" — then set it up again. You can offer two spoken sentences to pick between: "Is it 'that is my cup' or 'that is not my cup'?" A head shake or a one-word "no" is clear communication and is answered immediately, but it is not yet the sentence target.
make_harder: Let your child produce the negative sentence with no model. Ask for the contrast as two sentences: "That is not my cup. This is my cup."
group_play_line: A sibling can be the one who gets it wrong, so your child does the correcting.
what_to_avoid: Keep this playful and low-stakes. Never hold back something your child actually wants or needs in order to make them protest, and never keep up the pretence once they have told you — hand the right thing over at once. Do not use anything your child is already upset about.

title: I Need / I Want — Full Sentence
theme: Asking with a longer sentence, while short messages always work
materials: Ordinary moments when your child wants a low-stakes preferred item, activity, or turn that you can provide right away — a particular crayon, a turn with a toy, help with a game.
instructions: In an ordinary moment, when your child wants a low-stakes preferred item, activity or turn that you can provide right away, say the longer version of what they asked for: "I want the blue crayon", "I need help with this." Pause and leave room, then give them what they asked for whether or not the sentence got longer. Use these ordinary moments for practice, and keep them separate from essential, safety and self-advocacy messages. When the message is about stopping, a break, pain, the toilet, food, water, comfort, safety, or help with something difficult, respond immediately to whatever form it arrives in — one word, a gesture, a sign, a device, or a look.
success_criteria: During an ordinary, non-essential practice moment, the child asks for something using a sentence of at least four words. A short message about an essential, safety or self-advocacy need is NOT a failed attempt — it is successful communication and is honoured at once.
make_easier: Say the whole sentence and give a starter — "I want the..." Use a low-stakes preferred item or turn you can hand over right away. A two- or three-word request is answered and expanded, never withheld.
make_harder: Wait a little longer before modelling, and let your child build the request themselves. Invite one more detail: "I want the blue crayon please."
group_play_line: A sibling asking for a turn in a whole sentence gives your child the pattern without any pressure to copy it.
what_to_avoid: Never ignore a clear request to stop in order to get a longer sentence. Never delay food, drink, the toilet, comfort, help or safety for any reason connected to language practice. Do not require the sentence before access — say it, hand the thing over, and let the longer sentence come another time.
